img.alt: A honeybee on a honeycomb, with a dotted figure-of-eight path showing the waggle dance: a straight wiggly run in the middle and a loop back on each side.

qti-stimulus-body.p: A honeybee hive can be home to tens of thousands of bees. Some of them, called foragers, fly out every day to look for flowers full of nectar and pollen.
When a forager finds a good patch of flowers, she flies back to the hive to tell the others. But bees cannot talk. Instead, she dances!
On the honeycomb, the bee runs in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side. Then she loops back and does it again, over and over. This is called the waggle dance.
The dance is a map. The direction of the straight run shows which way to fly, compared with the Sun. The longer the waggle lasts, the farther away the flowers are.
Other bees crowd around the dancer and follow her moves. They also smell the flowers on her body. Then they fly off to find the food themselves.
Scientists worked out what the dance means about a hundred years ago, by watching bees in hives with glass walls. One of them, Karl von Frisch, later won a Nobel Prize for the discovery.
